utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Williams, may I remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you gave yesterday at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, sir, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic. Mr. Kuzmanovic is counsel for Mr. Markac. Mr. Kuzmanovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, during your testimony, you were asked several questions about your involvement and observations during the course before and after Operation Storm, and on page 24 of yesterday's transcript, line 7, you were asked: "What made you believe that the Croatian special police were involved?" And your answer was: "I had no evidence Croatian special police were involved." When we look at P927, which is your supplemental information sheet of 23 September 2008, if you have that in front of you, sir, feel free to refer to it. If you could pull that up, please, Mr. Registrar, page 2. But before we get to that, sir, did you know that the special police of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Croatia was part of the -- a lawful part of the Ministry of Interior?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I knew that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you aware that the special police was one of three branches of the police within the Ministry of Interior?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I'm aware of that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: What were the other two branches of the police?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Within the Ministry of the Interior or do you mean the Croatian government?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, within the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I don't recall offhand. My only familiarity is with the special police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you aware of what kind of uniforms the special police wore?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I'm aware that they often had single-colour uniforms as opposed to the multicoloured camouflage or BDU, the battle-dress uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Where had you seen those uniforms?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I had seen them previously in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You hadn't seen them anywhere in the theatre of operations in Sector South?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No, I had not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: On page 2 of your statement, the second -- first full paragraph that says "page 6" at the top, in the centre you say, of that paragraph: "He did not see any special police in Knin on 5 or 6 August, but he does recall seeing soldiers dressed in single-colour uniforms and wearing black berets during Akashi's visit. He is uncertain as to whether these were or were not Croatian special police." Sir, it's a fact that you have no idea whether or not Croatian special police were in Knin on the 5th and 6th of August; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that special police were there or not; that's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So any mention you made of special police is a mistake?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Any mention I made of special police is an assessment, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: An assessment?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Based on what?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Based on the familiarity with the uniforms, and those from a distance looked like the uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever talk to somebody and ask them if they were special police?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I did not, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you aware that the special police at that particular time were 80 to 100 kilometres away?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I was not aware of that, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm listening now and then to the French translation, and the speed you develop is impossible for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will remind myself to slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, P925, if we can pull that up, please, page 6, at the bottom of page 6, here, sir, you're talking about being back at the UN Sector South HQ in Knin, and this is on the 5th of August. At the bottom of this page, you state, in part: "I was thinking that the HV wanted to make sure that we, the UN, stayed put in the camp, so that follow-up HV units and so-called Croatian special police could continue into town and conduct their activities unobserved." Now, this is the particular reference to the Croatian special police in which you said that you had no evidence that the Croatian special police were in Knin at that time; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And the same with the reference on page 7, referring to August 6th at the bottom of page 7, in the middle of the last full paragraph, you state: "The action against the UN was likely to prevent the UN from observing the town while HV and Croatian special police were looting, conducting selective arson and cleaning/mop-up operations continued." Again, you have no evidence that the Croatian special police were involved in any of that; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Sir, if you're asking me if I could identify these people as Croatian special police, no, I cannot, and I do not have any evidence that Croatian special police that worked for the Ministry of Interior were involved, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The last line here says you left Knin on 7 August 1995 in order to return to Zagreb. Were you in Zagreb then full time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That full time, sir? I'm not left. I left on the 7th to return to Zagreb for the rest of my tour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay, that's what I meant by full time.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So you left Sector South on the 7th of August?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: On the afternoon of the 7th of August, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: How did you return to Zagreb on the 7th of August?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I rushed to Zagreb in a UN helicopter to Split and then a UN aircraft from Split to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you involved in any assessments of activities of the Croatian military or any other Croatian formation while you were in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I provided a summary and attempted to provide an understanding to my Canadian commander of what had happened in the Krajina, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever return to Sector South after August 7th of 1995?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I did not, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: As a military intelligence officer, were you aware of how the Croatian military, during the course of Operation Storm, and I say "military" in a general sense, was split up and what particular forces went on what particular axis?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: During the invasion itself, sir, or during the assault into the Krajina, I became aware of which particular units were on which axes, and then as a postmortem we had a better idea after the event which units actually took part. We became aware of particular units reporting from the battalions, the UN battalions in the sector, personal observation, and other people reporting on the units, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what particular units were involved in the -- in Operation Storm coming down from the Velika Mountains?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know at the time or you just can't remember?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I knew at the time, but I cannot recall, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could pull up, please, P744.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Before we get to P744, sir, you had said that you were -- with regard to the special police, that they had single-coloured uniforms. What was the colour of their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, it was sort of an off-greyish/steel colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And what kind of headgear did they wear?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Berets.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: What colour?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Black, to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what kind of footwear they had?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I remember that it was not uniform, they were very -- what I though would be much more comfortable boots than I had on and much more efficient for walking.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: What colour?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I saw brown and black.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And what kind of weapons did the special police have?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Pistols, some, and I can't recall further than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Just a sidearm, that you can recall?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Just a sidearm, that I can recall, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. What channel is the French channel? I think I'm going to listen to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. We're now on P744 on your screen. This is something that was put together by you and Mr. Berikoff?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I collated all this information from a variety of sources, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to turn your attention first to page 4, in the middle of page 4. This is the 5th of August at 10.00 a.m. It says: "Evacuation of ARSK, 15 Lika Corps started. Destruction --" I'm assuming that means "destruction ."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: "... of ammo stores." As a military intelligence officer, can you tell me something about the ARSK 15 Lika Corps and where it was located?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: 15 Lika Corps was in Sector North of UN Sector North and was the operational command level for a variety of brigades in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Was it in and around the area between Gospic and Gracac?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, that sounds like where they were, sir, but I can't be sure at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, the destruction of ammo stores, where were those ammo stores located?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: There were a variety of ammunition stores that they had access to and were under their control. I don't at this time recall which ones those are referring to, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: More than one; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, this evacuation was toward Otric, was it not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, it was towards Gospic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Towards Gospic or toward Otric?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Otric, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you aware, Mr. Williams, of the strategic importance of Gracac at the time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you aware that the ARSK, at one point, was set to defend Gracac to the last man?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Further down on P744, on the same page, it says: "August 5th," again "1700 hours," and it says "a WDR." What does "WDR" stand for?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: A withdrawing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: "ARSK --" is that convoy?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: A company, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: "... company surrounded and entered a Jordanian --"

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Jordanian platoon position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: At the site WK823326. Where is that location; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Exactly, no. From the reference, I would say it's in the Jordanian Sector, but I don't recall what exactly the village name, if there was a name near that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Is that Pribicevac, does that ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No, sir, but I have no reason to doubt if that's what you say it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it at or near the Bosnian border?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: On page 5 of this P744 -- by the way, the company that you referred to, do you know whether that was comprised of tanks with transporters?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I had no further information than a company size, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: They weren't walking?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I have no further information whether they were walking or in vehicles, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: On page 5, sir, the top third of the page of 6th of August, 1110, if you can focus on that: "ARSK convoy of approximately 150 persons, 6 trucks, 2 guns, 1 tank and police vehicle, heading from RSK to BH." Where would they be heading from the RSK to BH, what location?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I don't have any other information on that particular report, and I don't recall which battalion had reported that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether they had to go at or near Martin Brod?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Martin Brod was one crossing point into Bosnia-Herzegovina, but I'm not sure if that's referring to that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: They couldn't go through Bosansko Grahovo because that had already been choked off; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So the only other logical place for them to go, at least looking at everything in context, would be through Martin Brod, would it not, if they were heading into Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: If they were heading into Bosnia and did not wish to go further north, then Martin Brod would be a logical crossing, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Later on that very next entry at 11.15, it says: "10 ARSK tanks and 200 troops reported heading to Bosnia through area WK 8232." Previously on page 4, the coordinate grid reference was A23326. Are we missing a couple of numbers on this grid reference on page 5?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No, sir, that was the grid reference I received. Sometimes the grid reference is not as precise when it's reported. We try to report with six- or eight-figure grid references. In this case, four, I can see your point, leaves a fairly wide area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. So these vehicles reported --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could I insist on small breaks, small pauses, between question and answer and answer and question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will struggle to do my best here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The wider-area grid reference, would this have been this particular group of vehicles heading into Bosnia through relatively the same area as the previous group?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That would make sense, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And as far as you can recall, Mr. Williams, you're not sure of what city, village, or county those grid references refer to?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No, sir, I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you leave at the same time as Colonel Leslie did on August 7th from Sector South?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: He was not on the same helicopter as I was, sir. So I'm not sure exactly what time Colonel Leslie left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that he left on the same day that you did?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I do not know that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any estimate, sir, of casualties as a result of the shelling of Knin, casualties in Knin itself?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Civilian casualties, sir, or casualties --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Casualties in general.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Casualties in general? I had no precise figures. We heard various -- from reports, various numbers, but no way to confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you give an estimate at all, as a military intelligence officer, on what the casualties were?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I don't recall that I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: At some point in time in 2002 or 2003, the exhibit reference is D329, Colonel Leslie gave an estimate of civilians killed as between 10.000 and 25.000 as a result of the shelling. Do you have any figure to -- do you have any reason to agree with or dispute that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I don't know where a number like that would have come from. I have no confirmation of that, but that number seems to me to be quite high, if we're talking about in Sector South, specifically in Knin, sir, or --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Specifically in Knin.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That number would be far too high, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: That number is actually completely off base, is it not, based on your observations?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: From my vantage point, I would say that number is somewhat -- was actually far too high.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: It's not just far too high, it's completely off base, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the point's been made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, although, Mr. Russo, you can say, "Question asked, question answered," but if Mr. Kuzmanovic has made his point I think is not for you to decide, but this does not mean I disagree with you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Why don't we pull up D329, just the transcript on page 2. Go to page 2 of that transcript, please. This was a July 21, 2003, interview of both General Forand and at the time of the interview, General Leslie, and he was asked specifically about shelling. At the top of this particular page, "L" stands for "Leslie." He's answering: "I'm a gunner. I'm an artillery officer, a professional, so I can comment on it with some degree of validity. This was deliberate targeting on a massive scale of residential areas. Why? Because, I believe, it was targeted to break their will to resist. And, by the way, it worked. It killed a lot of civilians, and we'll never know the exact number. But estimates -- estimates range from ten to twenty-five thousand dead." He did not get that number from you; correct.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: He did not, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any idea where General Leslie might have gotten that number?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I have no idea where he would have gotten his data, sir. His comment of "we'll never know the exact number," I agree with. The estimates I find somewhat out of the range of possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you had earlier answered one of my questions that I asked about the withdrawal of the ARSK. Just so it's clear, I believe you initially said that the withdrawal was toward Gospic, but we corrected it to towards Otric, O-t-r-i-c; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't have any further questions, Your Honours. Thank you very much, Mr. Williams.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kuzmanovic. Since the Cermak Defence has no questions, Mr. Russo, is there any need to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I just have a few brief follow-up questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Williams, you were, if you recall yesterday, questioned regarding your assessment of whether or not the ARSK would have had several levels of lines to attack as the HV came toward them. Do you recall that discussion?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I recall that discussion, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And you were also shown an UNCRO military information officer's report, and if I could ask Mr. Registrar, please, to bring that up. That's D819. In the context -- while that's coming up, in the context of Mr. Kehoe's questions to you, he showed you a Google Earth image with confrontation lines drawn, some in red, some in blue, and for the Court's benefit this appears at page 62, approximately line 5 in yesterday's transcript, which, if my math is correct, is 9583 at line 5. And you answered some questions there, Mr. Williams, regarding what you believe would have been done. I want to be clear. If you could explain to the Court whether or not you know if any of that -- in other words, if several lines of defence were actually put up by the ARSK.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Right, Mr. Russo, if I understand what you're asking is, do I know for a fact or am I speaking in the hypothetical. In yesterday's answer, I was speaking in the hypothetical. I did not have confirmation of those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And looking now at 819, if we could move to the second page of the exhibit, and this paragraph, of course, is an assessment of the reasons -- possible reasons for the rapid collapse of the ARSK, and I'd like to focus your attention on number 42, where it indicates: "Absence of a counter-attack reserve (armour has been observed only on first echelon)." Can you explain to the Court what "first echelon" would mean?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The first echelon would be the first line of defence so that an invading force -- this would be the first troops they'd meet besides the reconnaissance forces from the opposing side.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: What does the absence of a counter-attack reserve indicate?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The absence of a counter-attack reserve would indicate that once the first echelon were to be breached, there would be no reserve armoured forces to counter-attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Does that mean that the HV only had one line to break on its way in?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object. Leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm asking him if that's what it means. It's not a leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, if you're asking him what it means, then ask him what it means, instead of already suggesting what it may mean, because that's what makes it leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: What does it mean, Mr. Williams?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Russo. What does what mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: The fact that there's no counter-attack reserve, what does that mean the HV would face on its way towards its objective?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The lack of counter-attack reserve would mean once the HV or HVO had broken through the first echelon of the ARSK, that they should not encounter any further armoured, if there was no reserve.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And do you have or did you receive any information to indicate that the assessment made here, which I understand is not your own, did you have any information to indicate that the information of there being no counter-attack reserve and armour only on the first echelon, do you have any information that that is not correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I have no way of confirming whether this assessment is correct or incorrect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: An assessment always exists of two elements. The first one is the factual basis of it. The second one is whether the assessment -- whether the explanation, even if the facts are correct, whether the explanation is correct. If you say that you have no way of confirming this assessment, were you referring to the factual basis of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm referring to the factual basis. The absence or presence of armour I have no way of confirming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Let's turn to your second statement, Mr. Williams, which I believe is P925. It should be the second tab in your notebook, and if we go to, I believe, that it's page 3, and that's where you discussed your trip up to Strmica and also your observations in Knin on the 3rd of August, and it discusses there on the top paragraph some of what you saw on your way to Strmica. The middle of the top paragraph there, it indicates: "On our way up to Strmica, we saw only temporary ARSK check-points, two ARSK M-84 tanks and one ARSK APC in position. This was halfway to Strmica. We did not see any troops or artillery. I remember that I was thinking that the deployment of the tanks was very unprofessional and that I had expected to see more troops in the area." Can you explain first what was it about the deployment of the tanks that was unprofessional?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I saw the -- in particular, the two M-84 tanks deployed in positions where advanced tanks such as this is being used as a pill box inside a house where the limit of main artillery fire, main gunfire, was restricted. So there was very restricted visibility from the house and the ability to move out of there in a hurry, so I thought it was a -- it was left there as a pill box. And there were no troops in the area to actually defend or to assist should infantry attack the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Russo. One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one short question for you. When you left in the helicopter on the 7th, was that helicopter in any way, as far as you could observe, inspected by Croatian forces or authorities?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No, it was not, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kehoe, you were on your feet. Any need to put further questions to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just very briefly. Further Cross-examination by Mr. Kehoe:

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Colonel, yesterday, taking this from redirect, I was talking to you about the artillery positions of the ARSK, and I was talking to you about the artillery being at three levels, at a battalion level, at a brigade level and at an operational level. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I recall that, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, you were aware of the fact that the ARSK had artillery?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I was aware of that, yes, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Do you know where that artillery was deployed?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Were you ever shown the munitions depot of the ARSK at Guljabic [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I was not, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object to this. This doesn't arise out of my redirect, where weapons were stored as opposed to where they were deployed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, could you please --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where do we find it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection of Mr. Kehoe [sic] is that it does not arise from re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The inference from the re-direct examination was that the ARSK did not have capabilities to deflect the offensive of the HV, and my examination of Colonel Williams yesterday had to do with the levels of artillery and the fact that -- just asking whether or not he had seen Guljabic. He hadn't seen it. I'm not going to go back into it. Of course, it's the D715, the video of General Cermak viewing that. But the inference from the Defence -- from the Prosecution that the ARSK had no capabilities, certainly in artillery, are just simply -- that's the issue that's raised and that's what's being rebutted.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, the specific question put to Mr. Williams was with regard to counter-attack reserves, which, as he answered, is troops to attack, not weaponry sitting in a depot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The takeoff point from Mr. Russo's question, as he knows full well, was the questions I had of Colonel Williams concerning the structure of the three levels of artillery support that was in -- up on the Dinara on the 4th and the 5th.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, we're talking about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your questions, as they were put, do not arise sufficiently and directly from the re-examination, therefore would you please move on, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: One last issue -- thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: One last issue with regard to Strmica. You were there, I take it, on the 2nd or the 3rd of August as you were driving around. Were you aware, Colonel, at that time, from your intelligence-gathering, that the ARSK was moving towards Grahovo to counter-attack and retake the ground that was lost? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT SCHUMAN WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I spent approximately 20 minutes at Strmica on the ground on the 3rd of August. I was not aware that the ARSK was planning a counter-attack, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kehoe. Other Defence counsel, no questions. Then, Mr. Williams, this concludes your testimony. I'd like to thank you very much for having come a long way to The Hague and for having answered all the questions put to you by the parties and by the Bench. I wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, would you please escort Mr. Williams out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm looking at the Prosecution. Is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness, and will it be you, Mr. Hedaraly, or --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, it will be Mr. Hedaraly. I would seek the leave of the Chamber to excuse myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There's no pending issues as far as exhibits are concerned for the last witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I didn't hear you without my earphones on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There's nothing as far as exhibits are concerned, in view of the last witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: There is not, Your Honour, only the, I believe, uploading of the sections of the Sekulic book, which I believe is something we can work out without the Court's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe we can work with Mr. Monkhouse to straighten that issue out, with regard to uploading what particular portions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, there are two elements: The technical part of it but also, what is sufficient context, and there, of course, I would expect the parties to -- that you would consult Mr. Russo and say, "One page, would that do," or I have no idea whether it would be appropriate for you to take one page or two pages or three. That depends on the context. Mr. Russo, you're excused.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. The Prosecution would like to call Mr. Eric Hendriks as its next witness, and Mr. Hendriks has requested to testify in Dutch, and so we have Dutch interpreters in the booth occupied by the Albanian interpreters usually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, which means that there are even more interpreters that you should take care of that they do not get into difficulties, and I'll listen to all the languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, while we're waiting for the witness, I don't know if we can deal with the Prosecution's motion to add the 13 exhibits to its 65 ter list. I know it was filed late so only the Markac Defence had time to respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there an objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I do believe we did respond, and we didn't object. Of course, we do have objections to the admission. Adding it to the 65 ter list is step 1; admission is something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So no objection against adding it to the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: No objection from the Cermak team either, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which means that leave is granted to add the 13 documents to the Rule 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And one further thing, maybe for the expediency, if we could have Mr. Registrar already assign numbers to the ones that are referred to in the statement, at least of the numbers 2 to 24, which were already on the 65 ter list and referred to in the statement. I will refer to some of those so that could be useful, if that is possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar is invited to prepare a list for that, I take it, and not to deal with it already at this moment. Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have an exhibit list for this witness that was provided. Some of the documents in his exhibit list are already marked as exhibits, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think there are nine which were already admitted into evidence as exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Your Honour. And just so we can have further benefit, if we can get the numbers e-mailed to us at some point in time so during cross we can smoothly refer to them. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Hendriks, sir. And I won't speak any more Dutch, because the official languages of this Tribunal are English and French. [In English] Mr. Hendriks, before you give evidence, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is now handed out to you by Madam Usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Herewith I declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hendriks. Please be seated. I take it that the parties take no issue with the Dutch text which doesn't require a solemn declaration but just a declaration, but it's the same for Mr. Hendriks, I take it. Mr. Hedaraly, please proceed. Mr. Hendriks, Mr. Hedaraly is counsel for the Prosecution, and he'll be the first one to examine you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Hendriks.

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Could you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: My name is Eric Hendriks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And what is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: I now work in a mortuary.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could we please have 65 ter 5470 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. Hendriks, do you recall providing a witness statement to the Office of the Prosecutor that you signed on 4 April 2008, and it was based on an interview on 27 March 2008?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And did you have a chance to review this statement yesterday?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And if you look at the screen in front of you and scroll down to your signature, is that the statement that we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Does this statement accurately reflect what you said to the Office of the Prosecutor in the course of your interview?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And are the contents of this statement that you signed true, to the best of your knowledge and recollection?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Finally, Mr. Hendriks, if you were asked the same questions today that you were asked in that interview, would you give the same answers?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would like 65 ter 5470 be admitted into evidence pursuant to Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Mr. Registrar, that will be number ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P931, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P931 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: At this time, Your Honour, I would also like to seek admission of the 27 documents that are discussed in the statement, pursuant to 92 ter, four of which have just been added to the 65 ter list recently, and I can read those out. That is 65 ter 5471, 65 ter 5472, 65 ter 5473, and 65 ter 5474. And just for the record, nine of these are already in evidence, so it should be 18 new documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Already in evidence, I see. Yes, we see them on your list, which certainly will assist Mr. Registrar to prepare a further list, provisionally assigning exhibit numbers to them. Objections in relation to these documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: They came kind of quickly. I think we -- I think I got it correctly. It's 5471 and 5472 and 5473 are the photographs. Is that right, Counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We certainly have no objections to that, and I think that 5474 is the 11 September ECMM report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. There's no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Team K1.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Team K1.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We have no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections against any of the other documents, which means that they are all admitted. Mr. Registrar will provide a list wherein we'll find the not-yet-exhibited documents to which provisionally exhibit numbers are assigned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may just, Judge, I mean, I don't know if I -- you said, "There are no objections against any of the other documents." Are we talking about the array of documents that are listed in the report or just these four?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I think, as a matter of fact, that you are seeking -- you are tendering all of the documents, and you just mentioned those who were added to the list recently.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm only tendering those that are referred to in the statement, so those are the 24 -- 2 to 24 which were on the 65 ter list and the four I've mentioned that we've added to the 65 ter list. I don't yet have a foundation to admit the other remaining nine documents that were not referred to in the witness's statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, is it clear to Mr. Registrar which ones are referred to on the statement, because that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar will wait to receive a list of those documents referred to in the statement, which means that he doesn't have to verify all of that. Then he'll prepare a list, and then we'll decide on the basis of that list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Just one point of clarity on that issue, that there are several statements that are in the 65 ter list that have been admitted already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And with regard to, I could say, many of the balance, we do have objections to many of those reports, those ECMM reports. I am not, of course, discussing those that have been put into evidence already, but the others that the Prosecutor is now offering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You have now expressed your general objection against a number of ECMM reports. Let's -- once we have received that list, let's specify and then know for sure where the objections are. Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I just -- for our clarification, I have the exhibit list, and numbers 1 through 29, I believe, are documents that are intended to be used through this witness. Counsel, just so I'm clear?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: They are all to be used with this witness. Some of them have not been referred to in the statement, but that's why the exhibit list for this witness are exhibits to be used with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is that the last nine on the list?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is. So Mr. Registrar should focus now on the first 29 on your list, which includes --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: With one exception.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the one exception being ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Document 25 that is on the 65 ter list but was not referred to in the witness's statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So the first 29 minus number 25, and then you'll raise with the witness some or all of the remaining numbers, that is, the documents we find under numbers 30 to 39?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And 25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And 25 as well. Mr. Registrar, this might assist you in preparing the list, and it also gives notice to the Defence teams where to object as listed documents, and I take it that numbers 30 up to and including 38, plus number 25, are the ones you can raise your objections once they are presented to the witness. Please proceed, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Hendriks, for this little procedural pause. Can I have the usher give the witness a hard copy of his statement for his reference. Mr. Hendriks, I want to ask you some further questions about matters that are in your statement that I wish to clarify or additional matters that are relevant to the issues in your statement. The first thing I would like to clarify is, if you go to paragraph 4 of your statement, you state that your tasks as an ECMM monitor initially included monitoring the humanitarian and human rights situation in the area. Did you want to clarify that?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Our main task was, indeed, observing and reporting all sorts of political, economic, humanitarian and human rights situations in the area, so humanitarian and human rights situations was one or two out of the three or four tasks that we had as monitors.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you. Then in that same sentence, it says: "... and particularly to prevent and report the harassment of the Croat minority in the region." Would you like to clarify what you meant by "prevent"?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Well, it was our task, indeed, to go to the Croatian minorities in the area to ask people how they were doing, how they were living there, if there was some sense of order. So, actually, by our presence and by visiting the people in this way, the Croatian minorities would feel a little more protected in this area at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And when you talk about the Croat minority in the area, referring to July 1995, when you arrived in the region, how many villages in Sector South had a Croat majority?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: A Croat majority? Surely we're talking of minority here. And as far as I can recall, in the area that we had to patrol with our team, there were four or five Croat minorities present, so not the entire region but only the area that our team covered.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I just want to clarify, when I talk about majority, I know the Croat were in a minority, but the villages themselves -- that within that village, had a Croat majority, that's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Well, then I don't know how many villages there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: So what do you mean by "four or five Croat minorities present in the area"?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: The area at the time was a Serb area, a Serb Krajina, so the majority were Serb, but there were a number of villages where actually also Croat people lived. However, they were surrounded by Serbs. So in that area, they were a minority. That is what I meant to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: So when you referred to the four or five villages, do you recall if those villages, within themselves, had a -- the Croats there, were they a minority, or were they a majority in those four or five villages?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Probably, in the village itself, the Croatians were a majority, but they lived in a Serbian area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hendriks. And if -- and if I understood your previous responses correctly, you would visit those villages; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Yes, we did pass them and talk to people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And that was before Operation Storm, just to confirm?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And were you aware that in 1991, Serbs had burned houses of Croats?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now I want to focus after Operation Storm. You and other ECMM colleagues reported, and we have a number of reports, some are in evidence, some we'll talk about later, about destruction that you observed in various villages. Now, during these patrols in 1995, were you able to distinguish between houses damaged in 1991 and houses damaged during or in the aftermath of Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Yes, we could make that distinction.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And how would you make that distinction?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Houses that had only been recently burned down were much darker, burned colour, mainly in the wood of the roofs and the window sills. Houses that had burnt in 1991 were different in colour, and there was simply some vegetation as well. You could see the house had been abandoned a longer time since.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 5120 [sic] on the screen, please, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. Hendriks, I will show you a report of 22 August 1995 from Team N2. 4120, 65 ter 4120. Thank you, Mr. Registrar. If we can go to the middle of the page, there's a reference there to the village of Polaca. I don't know if we can blow that up a little bit. Do you see that, Mr. Hendriks? It says "Polaca." There's a coordinate, grid reference, and then: "... totally damaged by 1991 war, DPs returning." Now, is this an example of damage that occurred in 1991 and that you reported?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hendriks, is it fair to say that in your reporting, if you did not specifically mention that the damage was in 1991, that the damage or destruction reported was from 1995?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Staying with the issue of these Croat villages, and I'm not going to tender this one, Your Honour; that was one of the documents that are in the list that Mr. Registrar will be preparing for us soon. If we can now go to 65 ter 5085 [sic]. I'm sorry, Mr. Registrar, I meant to say 4085. Apparently I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And you will see on the screen soon a weekly report from the RC Knin to the headquarters on the 13th of August, and if we can go to the second page of that document, at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: The last paragraph -- I'm sorry, Mr. Registrar, I made another mistake. Can I have 65 ter 2069. My apologies. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That is a weekly report from the 13th of August. Now if we can go to the second page at the bottom, the last paragraph, and it says: "All teams in the former Serb-held territory have been continuously reporting that, apart from the Croat minority village of Polaca and the old Croat town of Drnis, almost all towns throughout the area have suffered much burning of houses, and some of the smaller villages and the towns of Donji Lapac and Kistanje have had every single building burnt out." Mr. Hendriks, do you remember if any of the four or five villages of Croat majority that you referred to earlier today were destroyed after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: No, I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: When you reported the destruction of houses or buildings in villages throughout the area, did you usually distinguish between the Croat villages, the few ones you mentioned, and the Serb villages?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Not that I can remember, because we travelled through the whole area and mapped as much as we could of what had been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: How were you going about that procedure of observing and reporting these villages that had been burnt?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: During the morning meeting, they would tell us which team had to go to which area, there to map what had happened to the villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And then can you explain for the Court what that means -- what that meant, to map the area?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: With the aid of a map, you would get in a car, go to the area, and say, "Okay, I want to go and look at this village or these villages." You would drive there, you would drive to the village, and you would, well, cross through it, covering basically the whole village that you could then map, and this would take you all day, and around 4.00 or 5.00 you would go back to base.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And what would you include in your reports?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: In particular, if and whether the houses had been burned or looted, and if we could speak to people there, in particular Serb people who'd been left behind, then we would do that. And from those people, of course, we heard all sorts of stories as well, and we would report them also.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And during this patrolling and reporting, did you ever refer to the 1991 census to see whether the village about which you were reporting was, in 1991, a Croat majority or a Serb majority village?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: No, I did not specifically do that, nor did I see such a list.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If I can have P815 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. Hendriks, we have seen some reports, as I said, there are others in evidence, listing villages where there was destruction. I want to turn to the document on the screen, and this is a special report prepared by Mr. Liborius on 26 August. The second sentence in the summary says: "A rough estimate is that between 60 and 80 per cent of the property in former UN Sector South have been fully or partly destroyed." My first question for you is: Can you tell the Court, if you remember, what was the criteria used for whether a house was assessed to be fully destroyed or partly destroyed?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Entirely destroyed, we thought, were buildings of which only the walls were still up, so the roof was off, the doors and windows were out, the floors were burned. Partly destroyed, we would characterize if the roof was partly burned or here or there a window was out, so criteria like that. However, they were not black and white on a list or paper. It was just common sense that you would use.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And based on your observations and your patrols of the region at the time, is that estimate of 60 to 80 per cent of the property being either fully or partly destroyed consistent with those observations you made on the ground?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: At the time, we described 60 to 80 per cent. I'm sure it must have been about 60 to 80 per cent, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Let me show you a few specific reports, the first one being 65 ter 5041 -- 4041.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Apparently I can't say 5 or 4 today. I apologise, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hendriks, some of the incidents I'm going to ask you about are already in evidence, so I will not ask you too many questions about them, and that is not because I don't care. It's simply to avoid duplication for the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I must object to the commentary.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. It's an unnecessary comment. Mr. Hedaraly, you are aware of that, I take it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If you look at the middle of the first page of this report, when it talks about what happened in the village of Biskupija, there's a reference to HV soldiers with skull insignia that are described as Diverzantia. My question for you is simply: Were you present during that incident?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: In your statement, in paragraph 21, when you refer to this incident, you say: "I particularly remember the 7th Brigade soldiers burning houses, without caring that people were observing them." Did you talk to these soldiers at all?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: I don't remember that. Probably not. We were just looking, watching from our cars what was happening, what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, you are referring to a 65 ter number where it seems that you said it's already in evidence. Would you then please refer to the "P" number or the "D" number?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That document is not in evidence. I was referring to the incident. There's a separate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Incident, yes. Whether an incident is in evidence is yet to be seen, Mr. Hedaraly. I was not aware of incidents being in evidence. And then this 65 ter number appears, and I tried to find it on the list, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: It is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's the third, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see it. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If there are any documents that are part of this additional ten, I will specifically reference them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I would like now to go to 65 ter 4120 again. We looked at it briefly a few minutes ago. And if we go a little down, there's a reference to the village of Guglete. Do you see that reference, sir?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And in the second page, under "B," there's a short description of this incident where you saw members of the 72nd Military Police and an INA truck and then a fire --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I object to the leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Kehoe. I think that Mr. Hedaraly is referring to what the text here says, and that should be clear to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, not exactly. I think Mr. Hedaraly said the 72nd HV, and it doesn't say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you are not referring to the text with precision --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: The transcript says "Military Police," Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, not 72nd?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: It says 72nd Military Police, and Mr. Cayley said I said "72nd HV," which would have been a mistake on my part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That being corrected, perhaps you could put the question again to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Do you remember this incident, Mr. Hendriks?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And did you take a photograph of the house that you saw on fire?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: I or my colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If I can have 65 ter 5472, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Does this picture accurately reflect what you saw in Guglete on that date?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If I can now go to P812, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And this is a team report from your team and two from Soren Liborius and yourself on the 23rd of August. If we now go to the second page, under "B" it says: "Kistanje: In the auto workshop by the INA station, a fire was lit at 11.04. Next to the place was seen one civilian bus with HV soldiers, registration number SI 253-AB, and a Renault car SI 354-S. As the fire was lit, soldiers embarked the bus and the cars left the scene."

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And were you present in Kistanje on that day?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That was a team report. Let me show you the corresponding RC report that was sent from Knin. That is 65 ter 5476. If we go to the second page of this report, under the heading 3(e), can you confirm for us that that is the same incident that we just saw in the team report?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Just staying on with this document, if we go back to the first page, at the bottom of the page, under the heading 2(e), it says: "Humo monitored the fruitless attempts of dozens former RSK inhabitants in getting Croatian ID cards in Knin, despite all the people were trying hard, commuting between police, municipality building, searching for needed data. ECMM was until now not able to watch one Serb with Croatian ID card." And my question for you is: Do you remember Serbs having difficulties obtaining ID cards?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Can you please describe what those problems were?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: We spoke to people who were, well, particularly outside of Knin in the small villages, and they didn't have any means of transport. They had to go walking to Knin there, where the ID cards were being given out, and they would get there and they would have to turn back without success because either things were not in order or people would just not do this for them. In short, those people did not succeed in getting ID cards in these instances.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hendriks. Your Honours, I would like to tender 65 ter 5476 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] If I may. Certainly, I do not believe that this witness is the author, and -- excuse me. The witness is not the author and certainly is not mentioned in any of these -- any of his reports. Simply because he can point to one issue that is consistent with P812 does not permit the rest of the document to come into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: First of all, he did confirm that there's one report that -- he confirmed another portion that is consistent with his memory, but beyond that, I think that is a matter that goes to the weight of the document, not its admissibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, this document that they are attempting to put into evidence, and this is the objection on many of these documents, has nothing to do with his particular team, and nor does it appear that he was the author of this document. And simply because he can point to a passage in a document to say, "Oh, that is reflective in yet another document, and I recall that," that admits the document, nor a passage in a document that somebody else writes of some other entity within ECMM to say, "Yes, I understand that individuals are having problems to get ID cards," certainly doesn't authenticate this document to permit it to come in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said "doesn't authenticate." Is there any problem as far as authenticity of the document is concerned or would you just say it does not justify this document to come into evidence? It's not entirely clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's a multi -- it's a multi-levelled question, and the question of authenticity, especially since we first got this in quite a redacted form, is driven in large part by who the particular author is of this document, and clearly this witness is not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Authenticity, as far as I understand, is whether this is a document prepared by the organisation at the time and a report which was produced by that organisation. Is there any suggestion that this would not be an authentic document, which means that it is a forgery or a --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Oh, no, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So that authenticity aspect does not arise; yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I have no indication that this is somehow a forgery or, other than the redactions that I've received, being a document that's been altered. My main objection and the underpinnings of this document is the complete inability of the Defence to go further as to, for instance, what whoever this author was meant by various items. The Prosecution has pointed to two paragraphs in a -- and I assume they want to do this in many of these documents, in a three-page document that wasn't authored by them. This witness then points to those and says, "I recall those incidents," and they are attempting to put the rest of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think your objection is clear. Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Do I need to respond, Your Honour? It seems to me this issue has happened before. I mean, we have on the record how these reports are created, that the team reports are summarised by the RC reports, so there really is no authenticity issue, and this is just a document that assists the Trial Chamber. The Defence is objecting on the ECMM reporting with other witnesses about what may or may not have been accurate in those reports, so for this witness to be able to point out that that was in his team report and later reflected in the RC report is an additional [indiscernible] for relevance. And, in any event, Mr. Kehoe's objection goes to weight, not admissibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is denied. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I add?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Kuzmanovic, if I have overlooked you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: It's okay. I guess I also join in the objection, simply for the purpose of this witness lacks the foundation to be able to have these documents admitted, since he's not the author of many of these documents and only refers to specific portions in which it's pretty clear that he hasn't -- you know, he hasn't written these portions of these documents. There's no question as to the, you know, authenticity of the document. It's really an attempt to get the whole document in when, you know, three-fourths or five-sixths of the document has nothing to do with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That goes to weight, as far as the Chamber is concerned. Of course, the Chamber will not, on the basis of such a report, just accept everything, what is in there, if we have no further information. However, this witness says that what he reads in this report is, to some extent, and he explained it, consistent with his own observation, and that gives it sufficient probative value for admission. Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Can I have that in evidence, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number P932.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P932 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have looked at the clock. One more document and it will be a suitable time for a break, if I have your permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have permission.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If I could have 65 ter 3067, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where I earlier said that the document has sufficient probative value, of course, relevance was not an issue and the probative value is always looked at in the context of Rule 89(D), that the probative value is not substantially outweighed by the need to ensure a fair trial. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. Hendriks, if we can focus on the bottom part of this report, under item 3(b), it says: "In the Plavno Valley, Team N2 observed again houses on fire in spite of the promise of General Cermak, who visited the valley yesterday, that burnings will no longer happen." Do you specifically remember this incident in the Plavno Valley?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And can you please describe for the Court what it is that you saw?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: What we reported? That there were houses on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And did you see who else was in the area?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: I don't remember, other than my team leader, my driver and the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Let me refer you to paragraph 34 of your statement, in which you say: "I specifically remember seeing soldiers in HV uniforms setting these houses on fire. They were there, walking around the houses, and houses would go on fire. And since there was no one else around, I concluded that they were the ones setting the fires." Is that still consistent with your recollection?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Yes. Now that you put it that way, indeed there were these soldiers there who we saw walking around there, and therefore, we concluded that these were the men who had set fire to those houses, because there were houses burning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hendriks. Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, after the break, how much time would you still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I think I will be able to finish within the next session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a break, and we'll resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, the assessment of the time you'd need was one hour and a half in total. It seems that you're --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: In the 92 ter submission, I had provided a revised assessment of around two hours. Obviously, it's at the Chamber's discretion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I may have missed that. I still have the one and a half hours. If you could find something in one hour and 45 minutes, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no. I'm just asking for efficiency, and I've got no complaints until now. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. Hendriks, we talked about destruction earlier. I want to show you a few specific portions of reports on a related matter. If we could have P806, please. That's an 8 August report, and if we can go to the third page of that report. At the top, under "B," it says: "Team Knin reports that, although there are many chapels destroyed, the Orthodox Church seems to be untouched and has a military policija guard outside." And just to be clear, if we go back to the first page of this report, that is the report from your team or from the RC; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that. It's a report from the RC.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Let me now move to 65 ter 4041, although we may have a "P" number now for it, which is P933. That's a 9 August report from your team. It's going to come up on the screen in a few seconds. If we look at the second page of this report, and you can see under "Humanitarian matters" it says: "Churches on the following locations were intact." And then there's a listing of four villages. Next to "Kosovo" it says: "On the door was put a sign, 'Do not touch, HV.'" Do you remember seeing such a sign on the door of a church?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Let me now move to P934. This is an 11 August 1995 report from the RC Knin which is going to come up in a few seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me. I don't want to interrupt. If we could -- I understand the "P" numbers have been given, but just for the speed, I have them referenced by 65 ter numbers. So if you could -- if counsel could give me that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is 65 ter 577?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You find the number always next to the new "P" number. When you refer to the "P" numbers, Mr. Hedaraly, it should be clear that these are provisionally-assigned "P" numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I thought there was no objections to the first list of 22 documents that were from the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was not entirely clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
