utterances.text: There are many objections to all of those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So let's deal with that at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, I said "provisionally assigned," Mr. Hedaraly, in order to avoid confusion in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour. The only point I would raise is that if there are objections, then I may want to raise the documents one by one. I will not refer to all of them, but if there are objections, then I may want to raise them with the witness, which is going to take a lot longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do have objections to it. When I notified counsel that there was no objection putting them on the 65 ter list, there was no statement that we objected to their admissibility --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: But that's on the same document --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me. This is two separate issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's not --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I do have objections to the documents as proposed by counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, D65 -- the 92 ter statement is now in evidence. Would you for the time being, then, except if reference is made to certain documents apparently shown to the witness, that they would at least be MFI'd out of these numbers, apart from what we finally would do with them, because I take it that Mr. Hedaraly's concern is that if they are not admitted, that part of the statement is somewhere in the air, rather than a meaningful statement for the Chamber. That seems to make sense. Apart from your final objections, Mr. Kehoe, do you have any suggestion, how to resolve that issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I may be confused. I'm sorry, I think I'm getting confused now, Your Honour, and I apologise for that. There's two separate sets of documents. There are the ones referred to in the witness statement that were all on the 65 ter list, for which we have not sought leave to add. I'm just wondering if Mr. Kehoe's objection are for those new documents. That was my understanding. If I didn't understand, then it's perhaps my mistake. But if it is focused on those ones, I understand, and that's fine, I'll proceed. But if it's for the ones that are already in the statement that has been admitted under 92 ter, I didn't understand there to be an objection to those ones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's be clear. We had on our list numbers 1 to --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, 1 to 29, minus 25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it's even more complicated. We had the witness statement who is now admitted into evidence; that was number 1. Then we have the numbers 2 up to and including 29. Now, we take off number 25. You took that out, which means -- let me try to do the math as well. 29 minus number 25. Then we have one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine that were already in evidence, which makes 28 minus 9 is 19 --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Minus the witness statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then we have to take off the witness statement, which brings us to 18, and these 18 now appear here on the list prepared by Mr. Registrar. Objections also against these 18?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then now I come back to Mr. Kehoe, as to how he would like to resolve the issue of statements referred to in -- documents referred to in the 92 ter statements which are entirely in the air if we would do nothing with these 18. Do you have specifics that you say number so-and-so on this list, that's where the objections are?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you already indicate the numbers?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, I will attempt to go through this on the 65 ter list, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The 65 ter list, as presented by Mr. Registrar. Yes, that's also a way of doing it. Then put that -- yes, Mr. Kehoe, which ones?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The first is 65 ter 4041.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 4041, number 1 on Mr. Registrar's new list. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, my counsel is telling me that that might have been admitted already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's admitted already, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's not in already, it's MFI'd, Judge. That's MFI'd at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll look at what status it exactly has. Objections against the others. Which ones, Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, the objection is 65 ter number 577.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, 577. That's number 2 on Mr. Registrar's list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I don't know, Your Honour, if you, in fact, want to discuss the individual objections to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if they are all of the same character, we can go through them and then you would do it. If they are all quite different, then I think we have to resolve the matter now so that Mr. Hedaraly knows what to do during the remainder of his examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I move on this basically because I thought that the counsel put this on his exhibit list, that he was going to go through these with the witness. So with regard to 577, provisionally given P34 -- 934, that is an RC Knin report. It's not authored by this witness, and I believe that to the extent that it's even going to be discussed, it's going to be discussed in one particular incident. So there's an objection to that. The next objection is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's an objection, just for my understanding, similar to the one we denied before the break in relation to -- or is it different?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, I think, Judge, we have to look through -- on these particular exhibits that I believe I'm going to go through now, and I have to make sure of that, there's a difference between team exhibits and RC Knin exhibits. As we just discussed, there is Regional Centre Knin exhibits and then his individual team. Well, certainly this witness -- if I can start on the first premise, many of the Team Knin exhibits he didn't write, but certainly the RC Knin he didn't write. And although his team may have had some participation or their activities are delineated in that report, there's simply no way for the Defence to cross-examine Mr. Hendriks based on information that he didn't participate in. So in that sense, it's denying the Defence the ability to confront witnesses with exhibits that are being introduced by the Prosecution during the course of his examination. It's as if this is just being thrown out there simply because it's an ECMM document and accepted by the Chamber as being true, with no opportunity for meaningful cross-examination because, with all due respect to the witness, he doesn't know. And most of these documents, I will be frank with Your Honour and the Chamber, fall into that category.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And could you precisely, then, point at them?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If they are all, then it is quite simple, or if you could say, "This one does not belong to that category." I see that we are talking about ECMM reports for -- starting with 577. It's the next one, next one, next one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: 2069 is RC Knin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They are all on the original list, apart from those already admitted. I see that on the old list, you started with 4041. That's an ECMM report, and then up to -- up to number 20, these are all ECMM reports, objections --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Of two different versions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Some of them are team reports of which he is not the author, and some of them are Regional Centre Knin reports of which he is not the author.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I will gladly go through the list for the record, Your Honour, of those that I object to for those reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any specific, more than what you've just told us, or is there somewhere where you say, this is -- well, this report is not beyond doubt an original one? Is there anything else, apart from the general objection to different categories you have mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: There is no authenticity challenge at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but there could be other matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My challenge is -- objection is what I outlined for the Judge, the inability to cross-examine Mr. Hendriks on these documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but now you're -- you're now repeating what you said. It's that and nothing else?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Important enough, but nothing to add on specific documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, I have not heard from other Defence teams, whether they join Mr. Kehoe in his objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I have nothing to add, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Same here, Your Honour. We join. Nothing else to add, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber denies the objection against admission and will admit into evidence all the documents listed on Mr. Registrar's list, provisionally assigned numbers P933 up to and including P950. They are admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I hope that the time that we took here won't be held against me in the examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. Hendriks, we were talking about a few documents where there were churches that had not been destroyed, and we have now in front of us one more of these documents. If we can go to -- I'll just find it myself here -- the second page of the document, and towards the right -- towards the bottom half, right above "Humanitarian human rights matter," there is a part that discusses what happened -- what you saw in Grahovo. It says: "The team then went to explore Grahovo, the scene of heavy shelling and the site of HV occupation on 28th of July. They found the town almost completely levelled due to the amount of shelling and only the Orthodox Church still undamaged." My question for you is: Do you remember seeing the Orthodox Church in Grahovo being undamaged?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Yes, I have seen that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: There are more of these. I won't go through all of them. Let me show you 65 ter 5480. And this is a 9 September 1995 report on cultural heritage in the former Krajina. First of all, can you confirm that you prepared this report?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: I probably did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And based on this report and on your observations, was it a common pattern that you observed, after Operation Storm, that churches were not destroyed?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Yes, that was a common pattern.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Earlier --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just get clarity. "Churches" being Orthodox churches or Catholic churches?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I can re-ask the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: When you talk about the churches, it's Orthodox churches, specifically?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: [In English] I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And earlier you testified that 60 to 80 per cent of the property, you agree with that assessment, was destroyed, so that 60 to 80 per cent obviously excluded Orthodox churches; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me. I believe the witness said he couldn't remember about the -- with all due respect, the question of the churches, whether it was Orthodox or Catholic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it would be a general reference to churches, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That's a fair point. I'll re-ask the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: So earlier you testified that 60 to 80 per cent of the property, you agreed with that assessment, was destroyed, so that 60 to 80 per cent obviously then would exclude churches; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 60 to 80 per cent was all buildings, houses, including churches. So whether it was exactly 60 to 80 per cent of the churches, I don't know. Here, I see a list of churches, and whether those are Catholic churches or Orthodox churches, I have no idea. Just a general list. Those churches in those villages were, yes or no, destroyed and/or damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: But you just testified earlier, and I want to make sure that it was accurate, that as a common pattern, based on your observations, in large part churches were left undamaged. Have I understood that correctly?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, most of the churches were left undamaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, I'd like to tender 65 ter -- I lost the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President -- into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Based on the fact that he's the author, no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number P951.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P951 is admitted into evidence. I have to add that where earlier I denied the objection against the admission of P933 up to and including P950, that the Chamber considers that it's a matter of weight rather than admissibility, and that the probative value is not outweighed by the need to guarantee a fair trial. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Before I move on, let me ask you, Mr. Hendriks, about the reporting. The reports from your team were sent to the RC Knin; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And then the reports at the RC Knin would be sent to the headquarters in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And would you review the reports that were sent from the RC to the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Usually.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And why would you do that?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Of course, I was interested in what aspects from my report were sent on to headquarters; in other words, did I not work for nothing all day, and in which way is it being reported to headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: When you reviewed these RC reports to the headquarters, did you ever notice anything that was inconsistent between your team reports sent to the RC and these RC reports sent to the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: No, not really. Sometimes the method cut-and-paste was used for my report or our reports, and sometimes it was a kind of summary of what we mentioned in our reports, but there was -- there was no -- the truth was not violated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Let me go to 65 ter 4202, which is now P945. This is a 6 September team report from your team to the RC. And if we go to the second -- just to confirm, there was a reorganisation at some point after Operation Storm, and you moved from Team N2 to Team K1; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: The figures changed. On November 2 -- I was in November 2, and that was later called "Kilo 1."

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And if we go on to the second page of this report, at the last point before "Humanitarian" -- up at the top of the page, the last point before "Humanitarian and Human Rights Issues" it says: "At 1500 hours on the way Knin-Drnis, we saw for the fifth time in 10 days the Renault SI-821-BC driving with looted goods." Now, I want to show you the RC report for that same day, and that is 65 ter 5477. And if we look at item 4(b), it summarises some findings from Team Knin and says "also observed burning houses." And in the next sentence: "Also looting activity is in process, becoming more and more organised, as the same transportation vehicles were observed for several times in the area." Now, does this RC report summarise the findings that you have made that we saw in your team report?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to tender 65 ter 5477 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's the same objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Same objection. For the same reasons, denied. Mr. Registrar, that would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P952, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 952. P952 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you. And while we're on reporting, can we go to P766, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hendriks, while we're on reporting, this is a report from 26 August from Team N3, which is another monitoring team; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And am I correct in assuming that you did not prepare this document?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: No, I did not prepare this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now, looking at this report, is it consistent with the general reporting practice from monitoring teams at ECMM?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Well, I think the regular format was used, the format that we always used.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hendriks. Let me change topics now, and I want to take you back to 7 August 1995, the first day when you left the UN camp after Operation Storm and went back into the town of Knin, and I want to clarify something in paragraph 18 of your witness statement. When you went back in town, did you go to the ECMM RC building or to your own accommodation?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Both accommodations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And which one did you go to first, the RC building or your -- or where you were living?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I think we first went to the RC building, after which I went to the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: When you say "we went to the RC building," who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Mr. Liborius and Stig Marker-Hansen, and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And on that day, did you go inside the RC building with them?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And did you see any Croatian soldiers in the RC building?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And just to clarify that, do you -- when you say you don't recall, are you saying that you know for a fact there were no soldiers or that you have no memory of it either way?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I object to the leading. "I don't recall," is, "I don't recall." I think the answer was quite clear. I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness may answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Did you understand my last question that I asked you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's see.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A question was put to you, "And did you see any Croatian soldiers in the RC building?" You then said, "I don't recall." Mr. Hedaraly seeks clarification to the extent whether you do recall that there were not, which appears not to be your answer, or whether you just don't recall whether they were there, which seems to be your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not recall whether they were there. They may have been there, but I have no recognition -- sorry, recollection of that fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Let me move to paragraph 12 of your statement, where you refer to ARSK soldiers in Knin on rotation. And then you go on to explain that term: "What I meant by this is that there were ARSK soldiers in the town of Knin, but they were just hanging around and merely drinking. It wasn't as if they were part of a unit from Knin. I assumed that these were soldiers that were on leave from the frontlines, and I further assumed that these soldiers only would be rotated so that different soldiers would be on leave in Knin at different times." And the last sentence: "I can confirm that I did not see any ARSK heavy artillery or tanks in or around Knin." We'll just pause for the translation. Now, Mr. Hendriks, these soldiers that you saw in Knin, did they appear to you to be defending the town?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If we move a few paragraphs down to paragraph 14, and there is a reference to some shells that fell very close to where you were. And my question for you is: What's the basis for your knowledge that they fell close to you? Was it from the sound, from the damage?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Especially the -- especially the sound.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Did you notice any damage, when you got out of the RC building on the 4th of August, around you?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: When we left the RC building, we drove to the UN barracks, and en route we did see some damage, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And then in the next paragraph, 15, you talk about the residential building that was damaged. If we can have 65 ter 5471, which is now P947, on the screen. And in your statement, you talk about -- those are the two residential buildings that you refer to; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And you had a clarification to make, and I should have made it earlier. I apologise. In the last sentence of paragraph 15, you said: "Having observed the building, it appeared to me that it was damaged due to fire caused by a shell hitting the building." Would you like to make that clarification now?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: I looked at those pictures carefully, based on the questions that you put to me, and I wondered by myself how were they damaged. Was it through artillery, or was it through fire, or was it a combination of the shelling and a fire as a result? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: After the 7th of August, when you started patrolling again, did you notice any buildings on fire in Knin itself?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Some buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And if we move to paragraph 17 on your -- of your statement, in the middle of the paragraph you say: "I saw on many occasions that we were stopped while other civilian and military vehicles were allowed to go through the check-points." And then a few lines down: "I did notice that the police seemed to be acting more professionally after the Varivode incident that occurred on 28 September 1995." Just before I move on, can you just very briefly tell the Court what you mean when you refer to the Varivode incident?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Before the incident, it seemed as if the tasks of the police on the spot was not professional, whereas after the incident we saw that the check-points were manned in a more serious manner and that, for instance, the chief of police, whom we talked with, acted and said that he would really take matters in hand. So the general impression was that something would change in the attitude of the local police, but that was reduced later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you. My question wasn't that clear. That was my next question, but the question I wanted to ask you before that was: The Varivode incident itself, what was it, just briefly?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Briefly, the Varivode incident, I think some nine people had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And if we can go to 65 ter 5483. This is a 9 October 1995 report from your team, Team Knin, and the first paragraph under "General Situation" says: "The stronger Croatian police patrolling after the Varivode massacre seems to improve the security situation. However, little is left to protect and it is clear that this new policy is the result of international pressure rather than was a planned move." Is that consistent with your recollection?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, can we have 65 ter 5483 into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's the running objection, Judge, same objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: This is actually from Team Knin, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's the same objection, Your Honour. There's no indication he wrote it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is denied on the same grounds. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number P953.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P953 is admitted into evidence, and I took it that the objection was shared by the other Defence teams. Mr. Hedaraly, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you. If I can have 65 ter 5474 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's P950 at this moment, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Yes. I was just informed of the same thing by my case manager. My mistake. If we can go to the second page of that report, towards the bottom, just before the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: It says: "Five days ago, one man was beaten by a uniformed and armed man, who was shouting at him, 'Chetnik, go away. This is not your country.' Therefore, the man hides himself during the whole day." Mr. Hendriks, do you have a specific recollection of this incident?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And just to be absolutely sure, it says "uniformed man." What kind of uniform was he wearing?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Possibly a Croatian Army uniform, but I did not describe it in the report, so I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And then the next sentence at the beginning of the next paragraph says: "During our patrol in Vukse, we found two recently-shot dead women; one was shot in the back of the head and the other was shot in the belly and in the right side of the body." Do you remember actually discovering these bodies yourself?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I want to look at the CC reports, so after the reorganisations your report would go to the CC and then to the headquarters; and that's 65 ter 5481.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I seek one clarification in relation to one of the previous answers. You were asked what kind of uniform he was wearing, and you said, "A Croatian Army uniform," although you were not certain, since you did not describe it. Did you say that it possibly or probably was a Croatian Army uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Probably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I see I may have misspoken again. If we can have 65 ter 5481 on the screen, please. I'm looking, Mr. Registrar, for 65 ter 5481. I may have made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're almost through your quota of mistakes, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Judge, I'll give him some of mine, in the spirit of collegiality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Be careful, Mr. Kehoe. You might need them. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Could we go to the second page of this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: So there's a CC report for the same day. Under 4(d) --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, when I have 65 ter 5481, I get a different document on my screen, so it may be yet another mistake on my part, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Other people are making mistakes now and again as well, Mr. Hedaraly, if this is of any comfort to you. Unfortunately, the Chamber cannot check 65 ter numbers. If anyone could assist Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It is the correct one on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: We have the right one now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If we go to the second page of this document, so under item 4(d), and it says: "Team Knin discovered during its patrol in Vukse the bodies of two recently-shot women." That is the same incident you just described in your own report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to tender this document, 65 ter 5481, into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Same objection. This is CC Knin, not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The objection is denied on the same -- for the same reasons. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P954, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P954 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I would also like to tender from the bar table 65 ter 2821, which is a UN incident report about two bodies of two women that were discovered on the information provided by ECMM, and the injuries were the same. One was shot in the head, the other to the side of the thorax and stomach respectively, and this refers to additional killings numbers 305 and 306.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I -- we received notice of the fact that they were going to use this this morning, so at this time -- at this point, if I could just take overnight to take a look at it before taking our position. It could very well be that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it's tendered from the bar table, there's no need to decide on the matter in the presence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I just wanted the record to have the two documents together just for the convenience --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you'd say they are related. Defence will have time to make any submissions on the admission of this document, and then the Chamber will decide in due course after that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could have 65 ter 5478, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. Hendriks, this is a 7 September report, and this is from -- prepared by your team; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And let's just move to 65 ter 5479, which was -- which is your team report for the next day, 8 September.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Counsel. 65 ter 5479 is not a team report. It's a -- it's blocked out. Is this a CC report or is this, again, a team report?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: It says "From K1."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We just had the deleted one, so thank you for the clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: It says on the top line on the screen "From K1."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Disclosure had --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Can you just confirm as well that this is the report from your own team?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I have 65 ter 5478 and 65 ter 5479, the two team reports from Team K1 from 7 and 8 September 1995 admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No objection, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter 5478 becomes Exhibit number P955, and 65 ter 5479 becomes Exhibit number P956.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P955 and P956 are admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hendriks, all these crimes that are in your reports, the burnings, the lootings and the killings, did you or other ECMM monitors report those to Croatian authorities?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And can you please tell the Court who you reported to, who you reported those crimes to?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Either to the police chief or to General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And how often do you remember informing General Cermak of these crimes?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: A minimum of two to three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And do you remember what specifically you or other ECMM monitors would tell General Cermak about these crimes?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Yes. We talked about these types of crimes that had taken place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And what was General Cermak's response to you?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: The general would say that it wasn't good and that he would try to do something about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And from your observations on your patrols following these meetings, did you see any difference on the ground, in terms of crimes being committed?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: No, not really.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Can you elaborate on that? What do you mean by, "No, not really"?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Things didn't change.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: What things didn't change?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: The looting, the arson, those kinds of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And you also mentioned reporting these crimes to the Croatian police as well. Now, was that at the same time or was it separately from when you reported them to General Cermak?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: One time, we'd go to the police chief directly, and another time we'd go to the General, or both, because General Cermak sometimes said we had to notify these matters to the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hendriks. One last area I want to explore with you is the freedom of movement that the ECMM monitors had. We already saw a reference to check-points in paragraph 17 of your statement, when you talked about being stopped while seeing other military and civilian vehicles going through. Let me first of all show you P830, which is a 10 August RC report. And if we can go to the second page of this report, at the top of the page. Under item F: "Team Knin report the continuing ROM in trying to get to Benkovac and Obrovac. They were told by the policija on the check-points that they could only get to these places with the written permission of General Gotovina." Mr. Hendriks, were you present when the policija made that statement?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Yes, I was in that vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And did you hear that statement being made or was it reported to you later on?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: It was said in Croatian, and our interpreter interpreted for us that written permission was necessary by General Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Let me now move to 16 August 1995, which is 65 ter 5 -- no, sorry, I'm going to catch myself before it's too late -- 4085, which is also P936. And if we can just stay at the -- under item 2(b), it says: "N3 were again stopped at Vrlika check-point and was forced to do the usual Split visit. A strong protest will be given to General Cermak." Now, that's on the 16th. Now, let me just move you to the 17th August report, which is 65 ter 4094. And just at the top, under item "Freedom of movement," number 2. So that's the next day after the report we just saw. "Today we went to General Cermak to complain about the restriction of movement yesterday in the Vrlika area. He apologised to us for this accident that will never happen again. Military and civilian police should know that all international organisations have freedom of movement in the whole area." And then if we just move on: "The General reacted immediately by phoning the Minister of Internal Affairs." Now, Mr. Hendriks, were you present at this meeting where this protest was delivered?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And who was the one that made the protest? Was it you?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: It was my team leader, Stig Marker-Hansen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I have 65 ter 4094 admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... authors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The objection is -- I'm reading the transcript. It says "objection ... authors." You raised the objection, the same objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, there was no objection, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's unclear the -- Yes, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number P957.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P957 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Hedaraly, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you. So that's on the 17th, when the protest is delivered. Now let's move to the next day, the 18th of August. If we can have P511 on the screen, and if we can go on the second page under item C, "Security and Freedom of Movement."

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And it says: "Having waited two minutes at the combined Croatian MUP/military police check-point in Dabar and being told not to move, and to phone General Cermak (see the report from yesterday) requesting him to solve the problem of freedom of movement. This solved the problem, and after a few minutes N2 was back in business." Mr. Hendriks, you remember this occurring?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Not specifically, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Do you remember an instance of someone from your team, when your team was detained at a check-point, calling General Cermak, and then the people at the check-point letting you through?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: This is -- this is likely to have happened, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Do you remember if it happened once or more than once?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Several times, I think, this happens.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And let me now move forward to the 1st of September, 1995. If we can have P818 on the screen, and it will be the second page again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, Mr. Hedaraly, I'm trying to seek clarification of the two last answers. Mr. Hendriks, you said, "This is likely to have happened," and then you were asked if it happened once or more. Now, if it's just a likelihood, how can you tell us that it was once or more, because you said several times, "I think this happened." How can I reconcile probability with numbers, numbers of events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That likelihood -- I refer for that likelihood in that one incident that is in the report, and I'm not sure whether I was there, but this did, in fact, happen a number of times. Other teams and ourselves, we were sometimes stopped. The calls were made to General Cermak, after which we could proceed. I don't know specifically whether it happened at that date, but it is likely -- it is probable that it did happen also on that date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Likelihood is just about the one event that was put to you, and your answer that it happened several times is at other occasions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And with other teams, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And how did you learn this from the other teams? Did they directly tell you not only that they called but also who they called?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, because we worked in the same buildings and we would talk to each other, and these types of matters would be discussed either at the meeting the next day under the leadership of the head of the RC.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If I could have P818 on the screen, please, and this is a 1 September 1995 report. If we can go to the second page, towards the middle of paragraph (b).

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And it says there: "When N2 entered the very difficult accessible hamlet, one HV soldier rushed to the car and demanded to see the notebook of team leader N2. When this refused, N2 was told that N2 was detained on the spot until the commander of the soldiers could be present. Allegedly, he was out in the hills looking for the ones having started the fire. After having informed the soldiers that within three minutes N2 would call General Cermak, asking for an explanation to the strange situation. Then N2 was no longer detained." And, Mr. Hendriks, do you remember an instance where a threat of calling General Cermak allowed you to go through a check-point?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And did that happen -- how often did that happen?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: A few times.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Finally, Mr. Hendriks -- these will be my final questions for you. If we can have 65 ter 5482 on the screen, please, and this is a report from the CC Split of the 12th of September. If we go to the second page of that report, under item 3(c), at the bottom of the screen, if we just scroll down a little more - thank you - it says under (c), right above "4": "Team K1," and that's your team, "reports that per order from the Croatian Ministry of Defence only the Generals Gotovina and Cermak can deal with international organizations directly." Now, Mr. Hendriks, do you remember being told this?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: I understood the question, and indeed we were told that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And do you remember who told you that?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hendriks. Your Honour, that completes my direct examination. If I can just tender 5482 before I conclude. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections against --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The same objection, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The same objection is denied for the same reasons. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number P958.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P958 is admitted into evidence. I'm looking at the clock. Perhaps it's best to have the break now. Could we receive an estimate from the parties on who's first and what time will approximately be needed?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I will be first, Your Honour, and I would estimate an hour to an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Other parties? Mr. Kuzmanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going second, and I estimate about the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Depends on what the others --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Depends on what the others --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Judge. I'm certainly not going to duplicate the effort, certainly not try to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Being third means that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: There is a degree of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have a break and we resume at 20 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Hendriks. I'd like to take you back to an exhibit that was being referred to just before the break, and if we could have, please, Prosecutor's Exhibit 818 on the screen, and the second page of that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: By the way, I should have introduced you, Mr. Cayley. Mr. Hendriks, Mr. Cayley, who will cross-examine you now, is counsel for Mr. Cermak. Please proceed, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you look at the screen in front of you, please, Mr. Hendriks. Do you see the entry under (b), which is the entry that Mr. Hedaraly was asking you about before the break, and this is the episode where you were stopped, and after having informed the soldier that within three minutes N2 would call General Cermak, asking for an explanation, then N2 was no longer detained. Were you, yourself, present at this particular episode?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you said in your evidence that you remember a number of occasions when calling General Cermak, and you couldn't remember specifically any number, would essentially assure ECMM on its way. Can you now, from recollection, recall now, sitting here, any time when you personally called General Cermak and asked for his assistance in being able to move within the area of Sector South?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: I personally, myself, did not call General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, when General Cermak was being called in these episodes that you recollect, he was helping ECMM to move around Sector South, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He did help.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, in terms of anyone else actually calling General Cermak, these episodes that you're referring to, as you sit here now, can you recall now whether, let's say, Mr. Hansen, whether you recall him, now sitting here, ever calling General Cermak on the telephone to ask for assistance in ECMM getting on its way? I'm speaking now Mr. Stig Marker-Hansen. Can you recall any single time when Stig Marker-Hansen called Mr. Cermak to get ECMM on its way in Sector South?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Whether this was Marker-Hansen or Liborius, I don't remember specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let's have a look now at Prosecutor's Exhibit -- marked for exhibiting 935 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I thought they were admitted, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, they've all been admitted. I apologise. Then it's admitted Exhibit P935.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, if you could look, please, Mr. Hendriks, at the English version of this document. There's no author highlighted. In order not to waste time, I'm not going to go to your statement, but you do recall the phrase on the second page of rakija unloads being used, so you opined that it could have been one of your reports. Do you recall that in your statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I think that mischaracterises the witness's statement. He said that could have been from his observation from his report, not that that was his report. Maybe we should look at the statement to be clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We can move straight to the relevant paragraph. I don't think it's a matter of great importance, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there's any dispute about that --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I don't think there is. I don't want to waste time on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The paragraph that I'm interested in is where, in paragraph 1, you'll see that it states, in the second paragraph, that the military governor nor, General Cermak, is apparently the overall commander of the former occupied areas of Sector South: "He is being quite accommodating in his policy towards the UN and the IOs and has been very helpful with regards to freedom of movement." Now, in terms of Mr. Cermak being very helpful, was that something that was reported to you or was that something that you experienced yourself?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: I, myself, experienced this in the sense that at one time I was at one of those meetings in which we put forward all sorts of things about the burning and looting that took place, with also restriction of movement, and at the time that we mentioned this, General Cermak picked up the phone and called people of the Internal Affairs Ministry, I don't know exactly who, but he was willing to make sure that that restriction of movement was lifted.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So you personally found Mr. Cermak to be very helpful towards you?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: He said, "Well, I want to solve this situation. You must have freedom of movement." So in that sense, yes, he was helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, specifically I want to come on to the title of "military governor" that is used here. Were you aware, Mr. Hendriks, that in August 1995 no such position existed within the military and political structures? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, if the witness could be shown, please, Prosecutor's -- I'm sorry, Defence Exhibit 31.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, the Chamber has some expectation on what may happen now and would certainly not object against an expedited -- again, of course, we're not here to give the details of certain matters to the witness and to educate him, but rather to come to the point apparently you want to move at. I'm using these terms because, well, of course, we do not know whether our expectations are right or not. But in an expedited way, to come to the point you want to make, would certainly not bother the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, so that I can reassure the Chamber, I've had a long discussion with Mr. Kay about this, and, yes, it will be expedited. But when, of course, the evidence is brought for the umpteenth time before the Court, we do have an obligation to challenge it. I know we've made the point on many, many occasions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it's also the way in which it is done, and sometimes if a witness has not a perfect understanding, then if -- establishing that in itself, rather than to explore in full detail what the consequences would be for his perception of ... et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's very, very limited, but he does admit a document into evidence makes reference to the position, so I have to ask the question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Hendriks, you'll see before you a document whereby General Ivan Cermak was appointed as the commander of the Knin Garrison. Were you aware, when you were in Sector South, that Mr. Cermak was the commander of the Knin Garrison?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Not specifically of Knin Garrison, but we saw General Cermak as the regional military commander, let's say, so the person responsible or in charge of that area. Whether you call him a garrison commander or, you know, whatever, in our view he was commander of that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You are a retired military officer, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you understand what the meaning of a garrison commander is, being a retired Dutch army officer, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Yes, I know what a garrison commander is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you would accept, wouldn't you, that there is a very significant distinction between a military governor and a garrison commander, isn't there?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: I think that this would differ per country. In Holland, we speak of governor, for example, of the Royal Military Academy, governor of the Academy as such a person would be, and then there you have a governor of a capital city. We have operational commanders, regional military commanders and garrison commander. So in Croatia this may well have different implications than in Holland, but I did not, in fact, know that General Cermak was garrison commander. In our idea, he was the commander, therefore, the person in charge of that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, very briefly, do you recall how many municipalities Sector South actually covered? I know it's many years ago, but do you have any recollection?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: No. I would have to look at a report.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I'm not going to pull the exhibits out, but the Knin Garrison itself covered these municipalities: Knin, Nadvode, Kistanje, Ervenik, Olic, Kijevo, and Civljane. So seven municipalities were within the Knin Garrison. Now, to the best of your recollection, Sector South covered many more municipalities than those seven municipalities, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know the surface area of those municipalities, so I can't really answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So you don't know whether Sector South is identical to those seven municipalities or whether it's a larger area; you can't say now before the Court?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you recall how many military personnel were in the headquarters of Sector South, the military headquarters?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Do you mean the headquarters of General Cermak or of General Gotovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: No, General Cermak was not the commander of headquarters of Sector South, was he, so what I'm talking about is the UN headquarters of Sector South. Do you recall how many military personnel were in that headquarters?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: The UN Sector South consisted of, I believe, four UN battalions, and if you multiply that, you would easily get some 2.000 men, and to that you would have to add staff, but I don't know -- support staff, but I don't know how many people worked in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you know how many staff worked in the actual headquarters itself of Sector South?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: No, I don't know exactly, but there were, well, in particular, a staff, a sort of a brigade staff, and then you had the military UN observers, so probably -- well, you know, I would have to guesstimate. I don't think it makes sense to give you an exact figure here. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You're a NATO officer, a retired NATO officer. How many staff are normally in a brigade-sized headquarters?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Of a NATO brigade, you'd easily have 200 people, but this was a UN brigade, very different structure, very different numbers of people. So for the life of me, I wouldn't know how many military would have been working in that UN headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you know that General Cermak had nine people within his headquarters, within the Knin Garrison headquarters? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But certainly very different, in terms of size, when you compare it to a NATO brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: As to size, it is a very different thing, but a NATO brigade is not comparable to a garrison. You would have to compare such a NATO brigade to the division of General Gotovina. So, you know, we're comparing apples and oranges here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, let's move on, and let's take a look at P957. Now, I think, Mr. Hendriks -- do you recall seeing this document?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I'm not going to read it through again, because it's already been read through partly before, but I'm right in saying that General Cermak apologised to you over the restriction on movement; yes?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And I think he also explained to you that he was pretty certain or he was sure that a low-ranking officer had acted on self-initiative. Do you recall him saying that, in terms of stopping you at the check-point?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: I don't recall him saying that, but it is in the report so he must have said it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And do you recall him speaking with the Minister of the Interior and asking for the Minister of the Interior to make contact with the civilian police in order to ensure that this didn't happen again?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: He did speak to somebody on the phone. Who this was, I do not know. It was said that the Minister of Internal Affairs was that person.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And it says in the report: "The angry way of phoning the minister gave us the idea that he really wants to have a good relationship with the ECMM." Is that your comment there or is that Stig Marker-Hansen's, that Mr. Cermak wanted to have a good relationship with the ECMM?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: That is from the two of us, because, of course, we would discuss this in the car. This is a reflection of what we felt about this at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I want to verify one of the answers. One of your answers was: "He did speak to somebody on the phone. Who this was, I do not know. It was said that ..." And could you then repeat what you then said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was somebody from the Ministry of Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let's move on, and let's have a look at P937. Now, this is a document from Regional Centre Knin to Headquarters ECMM, and if I could have you, please, to look at paragraph 1(b), and the first paragraph, if I read it: "In favour of ECMM, the supreme commander of liberated Croatia (Cermak, the above-mentioned) tries to get freedom of movement to our teams and underlines this with an ECMM earwitnessed telephone call to the Croatian Minister of Internal Affairs." I'm not sure how the word "earwitness" will translate into Dutch, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's perfectly translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Hendriks, do you recall this particular episode or is this from another monitor's report?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: This is from someone else's report, but it probably comes from our report, the ones we were discussing just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So it's simply a reflection of the earlier report?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I noticed in your earlier report that Mr. Cermak is not referred to as the supreme commander of the liberated area. Now, I'm right in saying that you didn't hear Mr. Cermak being referred to ever as the supreme commander, did you?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You'll see here that Mr. Cermak is referred to as the supreme commander of liberated Croatia, and I'm putting it to you that you did not hear him ever referred to by this title, did you, as the supreme commander?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: "Supreme commander" means supreme commander, and he may not have been that, but this is about the Knin area, so I'd almost say what's in a name? He was the responsible commander in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let's have a look at P941. This is a report from the 31st of August, and I'd like you to look at paragraph 3(a): "Team N2 was informed through a letter from General Cermak about ROM, restriction of movement, in the wooden areas northeast of Knin, stretching to Bosanski Grahovo in an area 20 by 20 kilometres. All IOs are prohibited to go there due to cleaning actions done by special police forces. The letter states that the operation will last two days counted from today. Comment: Especially in this area, cases of human rights abuses were discovered by IOs in the last weeks." Do you recall this particular event and this letter?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Not the event, but I remember the letter that was shown us, and what is written here probably was in that letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Well, let's look at how these particular events developed, if you recall the letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can we have, please, Prosecutor's Exhibit 409. And, Your Honours, if I can just point out the date of this report is the 31st of August. That's relevant to this. And if we could please go to the -- if we can wait one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you recall General Forand, Mr. Hendriks?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: He was the commander of Sector South?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And do you remember Mr. Al-Alfi?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we can please go to the last page of this document, this is a meeting that took place on the 29th of August, so two days prior to the report that you've just seen. And if you look at the top of -- in fact, if you look at the very last paragraph, which is marked with a "C," and that's Mr. Cermak talking at a meeting with General Forand and

utterances.speaker: MR. AL-ALFI
utterances.text: "We are planning a large-scale mopping-up operation and will block the roads, but you will be informed 24 hours in advance. Could you please provide me with the additional list of people at the camp." And the rest is irrelevant for these purposes that we're talking about. But you'll note that it says there, "We are planning a large-scale mopping-up operation," and this is two days prior to the report of the 31st of August. If we could now please go to Prosecutor's Exhibit 410, and this is a letter to Mr. Cermak from General Forand, following on from the meeting that we've just seen referenced in those minutes. And you will see, and I won't read all of it, but General Forand is saying in the last sentence of the first paragraph, or the last part of the sentence in the first paragraph: "... I am unable to accept any unilateral restriction of movement imposed by your office in the area of my command." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And then, lastly, if we could please look at P411, and you'll see just at the end of that paragraph that Forand wants to be ready to consult at any time with Cermak about restrictions of movement. Do you see that in the last paragraph? Now, this is General Cermak's response to that letter from General Forand, and you will see that Mr. Cermak is saying that: "It was not my intention to restrict the freedom of movement of UNCRO officers, but draw your attention to the danger your officers might be exposed to should they happen to be moving through the area where we intend to start a large-scale mopping-up operation tomorrow to clear the territory of defeated enemy groups." Now, is this the letter that you recall seeing when I asked you the question earlier and you said you didn't remember the event but you remembered seeing the letter?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: No, I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But you can see in this letter that Mr. Cermak is making it very plain that there is no intention of restricting the movement of UNCRO?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Yes, that's what the letter says.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And in the ECMM report, of course, it refers quite incorrectly to the letter restricting the movement of personnel?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I think there's a mischaracterisation here. The witness just said he's not sure it's the same letter that is in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It becomes --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: This is the only letter we have from this time, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, and the letter read in its entirety --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, speaks for itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- speaks for itself or is interpreted by whomever reads it in the way he interprets that. Intentions are expressed here. Two intentions are expressed in this letter. Perhaps you could move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The letter that you saw from General Forand, the letter before this letter, had you ever seen that letter before?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Were you aware that there were renegade members of the army of the ARSK in and around the Sector South area at this time?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Not specifically, but if they were there, they could not influence our operation, in the sense we didn't have to fear them because we were a neutral party. We went around in white vehicles with white uniforms, so there was no reason for us not to be able to enter the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But specifically do you -- I mean, if you can answer the question, sitting here now, are you aware or are you not aware that there were members of the ARSK present within the Sector South area at this time at the end of August of 1995?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Yes, because General Cermak told us.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let's please look at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would seek clarification of the answer. You said, "Yes, because General Cermak told us." Did you have any other source which would provide you with information about, at that time in Sector South, the presence of members of the ARSK? So apart from, as you said, General Cermak told you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It could be that it was cascaded to us also through the UN Sector South, so I myself did not get that information, but probably through the head of our action who was in touch with General Forand, and that way it may have ended up within our team as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said "it may have ended." Is this speculation, or do you have any personal observation, or do you have any recollection of reports given to you about the presence of ARSK members at that time in Sector South?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not specifically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If, please, we could look at Prosecutor's Exhibit 946.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Paragraph 2(b) of this particular document: "General Cermak is starting a rather large action to stop illegal moving into empty flats, looting and arson, which was unfortunately most frequently done by HV members." And then it goes on to explain that ten warrants of arrest have been issued and that the perpetrators will face courts martial in Split, and that these are members of the HV who are putting the HV to shame : "They cannot remain in the Croatian Army." And then he makes explanation -- or the report makes explanation about units of military and civil military police have been enlarged in order to prevent such illegal actions. Do you recollect this particular event, Mr. Hendriks?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: It is quite possible that this was discussed during one of our meetings with General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Just to assist you with your memory, if we could look at D59.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, could we first seek clarification of the part you read? You read everything, I think, up until the brackets at the end, where it says "SL Dalmacija."

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm just about to deal with that, Your Honour, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could look at D59.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you regularly receive translations of newspaper articles, Mr. Hendriks?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did ECMM at all receive translations, not you personally but members of ECMM, did they receive translations of newspaper articles? Now I'm talking about local newspaper articles in the area in Croatia, in the southern part of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: I can imagine that the head of our action was interested in what the press wrote, and I think I remember that articles from the newspapers were translated on a regular basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could just go to the bottom of this particular article, and we'll see there an explanation for the purposes of the Presiding Judge. Can you just go a bit further, please, and you'll see it says "Slobodna Dalmacija." And within the original report, the Presiding Judge noted that -- I think it said "S. Dalmacija." You've never seen this newspaper article before, Mr. Hendriks, have you?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: No, I've never seen this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But you do recall the operation to stop illegal appropriation of apartments and looting and torching of homes in Knin; you do remember that?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: I said before that during discussions with General Cermak, this has certainly been an issue. So what the General declared to the newspaper, he certainly also told us.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you'll see, if you go to the top of this article, where it says: "There is no place for looters in the HV, in the Croatian Army," do you recall whether General Cermak also made that clear to you at the meeting that you attended with him where this particular operation was discussed?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Not specifically. General Cermak wanted to put an end to the looting. He said, "This has to stop, and I'll do my best to stop it." So whether he said that there was no room for looters in the Croatian Army, whether he said that or not, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have any further questions of this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cayley. Next in line, Mr. Kuzmanovic. You'll now be cross-examined, Mr. Hendriks, by Mr. Kuzmanovic, who is counsel for Mr. Markac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll just get set up, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: We haven't received any documents that are going to be used by either Mr. Gotovina's counsel or Mr. Kuzmanovic's [sic] counsel at this time, and I believe the procedure set out was that at the end of direct examinations --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps they would not use --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can take the blame for this, because I overestimated the amount of time, Mr. Hedaraly, that I was going to use, and I think Mr. Kuzmanovic has probably been taken a little bit unaware. So that's actually my responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I always thought it would be once the examination-in-chief would have been concluded and not once the previous cross-examiner has done his job. That is what is on my mind, so that the Prosecution is put on notice as soon as they have an opportunity to include those documents in their examination-in-chief anymore. That's what is my recollection, but if we have to verify that -- at this moment, it is as it is, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I have the transcript reference, because it was in the joint motion that the Gotovina Defence filed, so it's the 13th of March, 2008, at 660, and Your Honour's recollection is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, if -- I don't know how many documents you are going to use in the next 16 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: It's going to be okay for the next 15 minutes, but if for Monday we can have them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
