utterances.text: I can send them right now. It's just the exhibits that are being tendered -- that were tendered and the statement that was taken that was not tendered, 65 ter 2410.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And it was my understanding, just for the Court's reference, that each party, and this is how we've been doing it all along, sends their list usually toward the end of the cross-examination of the person in front. So that's what we've been doing all along and this is the first time we've had this issue come up. So I will proceed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's not make a drama out of it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you came into Sector South in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And you had three days of training in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Three days in Zagreb, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: What kind of training did you have in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: It was particularly dealing with the means of liaison [indiscernible] the whole situation in the area at that time, what was going on, but all of these matters I had heard about in the Netherlands previously during a course that we were made to take.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: What kind of a course did you take in the Netherlands before going to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: The course was called "The Monitors Course."

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And if you could just give us a brief description of how long that course was and what kind of curriculum was in that course.

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: We were given a course of English in order to improve our linguistic skills, and besides, we were told about the history of the Balkans, the conflict, the reasons for the conflict, how to deal with the population, how to work with interpreters, information on mines, all that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: How long was that? Was that a week, a day?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: [In English] Let's say three or four weeks. [Interpretation] Three or four weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, when you came to Zagreb for the training that you had there, you went to Knin, roughly, July 21st of 1995; correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: [In English] It was on the Friday. [Interpretation] It was on a Friday, the 21st, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, when you communicated with your fellow ECMM monitors, it was in English; correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: I spoke Dutch with the Dutch monitors, but there were also other nationalities there, and with them we spoke English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: When you participated in putting together reports, did you put those reports together yourself in English or were they in Dutch and did somebody translate them?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: I read them in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, we've had a great many of reports that have been tendered through you, sir. Some of the reports, the authors' names have been redacted. Would you be able to, between today -- after we are done today and tomorrow, tell us which of those reports that you wrote exclusively?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps I probably could identify several.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I would respectfully request that if you have those reports with you, sir, that you take a look at them. It might make things go a little faster tomorrow. If you could let us know which of the reports that you wrote, so -- and I will ask you some questions about those, if that's all right with the Prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Some of them, the answer is already in the statement, so I don't want him to duplicate, when he says, "This my report," or, "It's not my report." Second of all, I wasn't planning to be here tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't want -- I didn't want to draw your attention to the fact that it's Saturday tomorrow, but I think Mr. Kuzmanovic is also seeking whether it's a report exclusively drafted by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it's not -- it's not much work, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That's not the issue. Just for the -- I think everyone is aware the reason the names are redacted is because that's the way that we were authorised to use them by ECMM. Just so that the record is clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Understood, understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I just wanted to make sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, what is your interpretation of these limitations? Would they bind this witness, in your view, or was it out of an abundance of caution that the ECMM redacted the names so as in order to protect the persons, which might mean that we also would have to ask the witness whether he feels that he becomes more vulnerable if he would identify the reports he drafted or --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I would agree with the latter, Your Honour, but I think since he is testifying here and there are no protective measures involved, I would think it would be fairly simple for the witness to find which were the ones that he drafted, and we can talk about this in public session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's give it some thought on whether we -- the Chamber might want to further consider whether it will ask the witness, as you suggested, to identify those reports he drafted on his own.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I think it would assist in at least making cross-examination a little bit more efficient, Your Honour, from my standpoint, rather than having to go through every single report, which I really don't want to have to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, of course, efficiency is a great thing but would not resolve all matters. It comes into my mind to what extent providing documentation, already redacted, and apparently without any limitation in use, as far as the use as an exhibit is concerned, whether that would be similar to a Rule 70 situation, where of course a state can give material and say, "Don't use it as evidence, but only do so if we give permission." It's a bit -- it might need a bit more analysis, legal analysis before -- so therefore the Chamber will consider --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I do understand the dilemma, Your Honour. I think, in light of the fact that the witness is here and he's testifying and it's in open session, I think it's only fair, at least from our standpoint, now that the documents have been tendered as evidence, for us to know which ones he specifically worked on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At least we could already ask the witness, prior to further considering the matter. Mr. Hendriks, would you have any problem - you didn't give that impression - if you would be asked to identify the reports that you and solely you prepared?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, before coming to Sector South, what experience did you have with either setting up or dealing with check-points?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: I have some experience, because I worked in the Dutch land force, and they work with check-points as well, so I had some experience there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: What kind of experience did you have? Was it in Holland or was it somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: In the Netherlands and in Germany.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And these were situations in which there was obviously no armed conflict going on; correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: No, no armed conflicts, only drills.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you happen to have any experience in providing security to an area after a military operation?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: During those drills, such issues, of course, were practiced?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: But in terms of having to actually put that practice in the real world in dealing with an area in which there was an armed conflict, you did not have that experience prior to coming to Croatia; correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to refer to, please, 65 ter 2410, if we could pull that up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hendriks, this is a statement that you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor on April 18th of 1996. Does that look familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And your signature at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And if we could go to the last page of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, I have a hard copy, if you would want the witness to refer to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: That would be wonderful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, that statement is five pages long, and at the end of the page 5, are those your initials at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: On the first page of the statement, not the cover page, but the first page of the statement itself, which is on the bottom "page 1," if we can refer to that, please, you note in the first full paragraph of your statement, about a third of the way down, you didn't see killing, mis-treatment, or intimidation of civilians by the Croats. And when you made that statement, that was during your entire time you were in the Sector South area; correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Later in that same statement, toward the bottom of this first page, you describe the general military situation as tense, with a lot of ARSK soldiers seen in Knin town, and you have "rotation?" "And every capable military man was mobilised." Can you describe for me what -- the relative age range of every military capable man who was mobilised?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: Between 18 and 50 is my estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Later in that same paragraph, you note that: "We were not allowed to monitor the ARSK defence lines." How were you not allowed to monitor those defence lines? Can you describe for me?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: In the two weeks before Operation Storm, we talked to the military commanders of the Serbs, and they said, "No, you're not allowed to go on."

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And was that something where you would issue a protest to someone and -- how did you react to that? Did you just accept it as a fact? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: We did, in fact, because it was an area of which they said, "We leave those lines intact and no one has any business there."

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you try to find various methods to get around their prohibition to go to those defence lines?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: No. Why should we? It was not in our interest. We did not have to monitor that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Then what was the purpose of the statement that, "We were not allowed to monitor the ARSK defence lines," if that didn't interest you?

utterances.speaker: ERIC HENDRIKS
utterances.text: I think simply to complete our own picture for the report, that's why I wrote it down; a general description of the situation at that time. And I indicated immediately at that time we could not judge about it because we could not report on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I will halt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll adjourn for the day. Before we do, Mr. Hendriks, I'll address you in your own language. [Interpretation] Mr. Hendriks, I instruct you that you should talk to no one about the statements you have given so far, nor about the statements you will be providing in the days to come. [In English] I gave him the instruction in the language of Mr. Hendriks. We'll adjourn, and we'll resume on Monday, the 29th of September, 9.00 in this same courtroom.
